To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the British colonial governments of East Africa, West Africa, and Palestine held lower-yield, shorter maturity British securities and assets than would have been optimal for them to do.

(i) The Palestine currency board had a portfolio of securities and assets that was not significantly different from that of the West African Currency Board, despite the fact that the Palestine currency board had much higher reserves than the West African Currency board, and (ii) the East African Currency Board held a portfolio that was significantly different from the portfolios of the Palestine and West African Currency Boards.

the British government, in establishing and operating the currency boards of East Africa and West Africa, and in advising the currency board of Palestine, did so in ways that were beneficial to the British Empire.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following question: did British colonialism primarily benefit Britain or its colonies? We examine the assets of three currency boards, and find that they were not as profitable as they might have been.
a specific aspect of British imperialism: the establishment and operation of currency boards in Palestine, East Africa and West Africa.
whether or not the colonial currency boards in Palestine, East Africa and West Africa were used by the British as an instrument of imperialism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
British colonial policy benefited Britain, not its colonies.
, on the whole, British colonial currency boards did not act in a self-serving way, and did not cost their colonies any revenue, but rather acted to benefit the colonies.
the British currency board policy was designed to help Britain and its financial institutions at the expense of colonial governments and their people.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the British Empire was a net drain on Britain.
British colonial policy did benefit the colonies, but not in the way that Wadan Narseye claims.
the currency boards of British colonies held a portfolio of British government securities that were not optimal for them, and that this was the result of British colonial policy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the currency boards of British colonies did not hold lower yielding, shorter term, or more British securities than they needed to.
the currency boards were not a mechanism for Britain to extract value from the colonies.
the currency boards of East Africa and West Africa held a large share of British assets, but the currency board of Palestine held a much smaller share.
